scenes.recognized_speech: Parcels for the mail train are strapped in bundles of four, 17 parcels make four full bundles and one loose parcel. How many more parcels would fill that last bundle? Three, the remainder tells us what is already there, the gap tells us what is missing.
A parcel label earns a square stamp if its number divides evenly by 4, it earns a triangle stamp if the number divides evenly by 3. The four labels are 324, 344, 354, and 384, which get both stamps.

For the square stamp, inspect the last two digits. A hundred is divisible by four, so the hundreds place cannot spoil the test. 24, 44, and 84 pass. 54 fails, for the triangle stamp, add the digits. The three survivors have sums 9, 11, and 15. Only the first and last labels get both stamps.

A crate contains between 23 and 59 parcels, including both ends. Add one parcel. Now the crate can be packed exactly in fours, and it can also be packed exactly in sixes. How many different original loads could it have held?
push the whole interval one place to the right, 23 becomes 24, and 59 becomes 60. We now need numbers in this shifted interval that the groups of 4 and the groups of 6 both reach.

Mark the multiples of 4 above the line and the multiples of 6 below, both first meet at 12 after 0, the same arrangement repeats every 12. In our shifted interval, the shared stops are 24, 36, 48 and 60.

Each shared stop describes the crate after adding a parcel. Take one away from each. The original loads are 23, 35, 47, and 59. Four possibilities. Check the last one. The extra parcel makes 60, which packs as 15 -4s or 10 -6s.

Attempting answer keeps 60 and loses 23. That mixes two different number lines. Move the end stops when you change the quantity. Test the new quantity, then undo the change. For a different remainder problem, first ask whether one small move can make both divisions exact.

captions.text: Parcels for the mail train are strapped in
bundles of four.
Seventeen parcels make four full bundles and
one loose parcel.
How many more parcels would fill that last bundle?
Three.
The remainder tells us what is already there.
The gap tells us what is missing.
A parcel label earns a square stamp if its number
divides evenly by four.
It earns a triangle stamp if the number divides
evenly by three.
The four labels are three hundred and twenty four,
three hundred and forty four,
three hundred and fifty four,
and three hundred and eighty four.
Which get both stamps?
For the square stamp, inspect the last two digits.
A hundred is divisible by four, so the hundreds place
cannot spoil the test.
Twenty four, forty four and eighty four pass.
Fifty four fails.
For the triangle stamp, add the digits.
The three survivors have sums nine, eleven and fifteen.
Only the first and last labels get both stamps.
A crate contains between twenty three and fifty nine
parcels, including both ends.
Add one parcel.
Now the crate can be packed exactly in fours, and it can
also be packed exactly in sixes.
How many different original loads could it have held?
Push the whole interval one place to the right.
Twenty three becomes twenty four,
and fifty nine becomes sixty.
We now need numbers in this shifted interval that the
groups of four and the groups of six both reach.
Mark the multiples of four above the line,
and the multiples of six below.
Both first meet at twelve after zero.
The same arrangement repeats every twelve.
In our shifted interval, the shared stops are
twenty four, thirty six, forty eight and sixty.
Each shared stop describes the crate after
adding a parcel.
Take one away from each.
The original loads are twenty three, thirty five,
forty seven and fifty nine.
Four possibilities.
Check the last one.
The extra parcel makes sixty, which packs as fifteen
fours or ten sixes.
A tempting answer keeps sixty and loses twenty three.
That mixes two different number lines.

Test the new quantity, then undo the change.
